[Slides](15-scraping-slides.html) · [Live script](15-scraping.R) ·
[Source](https://github.com/ArielOrtizBobea/aem6850/blob/main/fall-2026/sessions/15-scraping.qmd) ·
[the project](data/15-scraping.zip)

How to get data out of pages built for people, in seven steps: when
scraping is the right route; the ways to collect a site (a saved page read
into R with `rvest` and CSS selectors, static and dynamic pages, six
routes to every page); what to take into account (terms, copyright,
robots.txt, personal data, a polite fetch); AI tools, in R or Python;
verifying what a scrape returns; a live demonstration in which two coding
agents, one in R and one in Python, collect seven years of a marathon's
finish times from the same brief; and laying out a scrape so someone else
can re-run it. The Federal Reserve's policy statements since 2006 carry
the code and both exercises.

**The project.** Install the packages once, in the R Console:
`install.packages(c("rvest", "httr2", "jsonlite"))`. Download
[15-scraping.zip](data/15-scraping.zip), unzip it, and open
`15-scraping.Rproj`, so that R starts in the project folder. It holds:

- `cache/`: every page the slides use, saved as the server sent it on
  18 October 2026: the meeting calendar, the fifteen year pages, 243
  press-release pages, the press-release list page and its feed, two
  Wayback Machine
  listings and one 2015 snapshot, a Wikipedia article's revision history
  and one Wikipedia table page. With these files every slide runs with
  no network.
- `fomc_statements.csv`: the file this session builds, one row per policy
  statement since 2006.
- `fetch_page.R`: the fetch function from the slides, with Exercise 2's
  two long lines as comments.
- `agent_run/`: what a coding agent was asked, what it wrote and what it
  produced, captured in prep.
- `wineglass/`: the demonstration. The brief, and each agent's scripts,
  file and figures from the prep run of 19 October 2026 (`r/` and
  `python/`). The results pages themselves are not included: they carry
  runners' names.
- `reference_scrape.R` and `build_statements.R`: the scripts that built
  `cache/` and the CSV.
- `SOURCE.txt`: each source, its address, the date of each request, the
  Board's public-domain line, and the rule that decides what counts as a
  statement.
- `mine/`: created in class by `fetch_page()`. Your own fetches go here,
  so the shipped pages never change.

## Objectives {#objectives}

By the end of this session you can:

- Say when scraping is the right route, after a dataset someone built, a
  download, an API or feed, and a licence.
- Say whether a site may be scraped from its terms of use, its
  robots.txt, copyright and the personal data on it.
- Read a saved web page into R with `read_html()`.
- Find an element's class with the browser's inspector.
- Pick elements out with CSS selectors, `html_elements()`,
  `html_element()`, `html_text2()` and `html_attr()`.
- Read an HTML table with `html_table()`.
- Fetch a page politely: a user agent with your address, one request a
  second, every page saved once as raw bytes, a fetch log.
- Read a server's status code and act on it.
- Tell a static page from a dynamic one and find the file it loads.
- Name six ways to find every page on a site.
- Write a brief for a coding agent: the unit, the start pages, the rules,
  the output columns and the numbers to print.
- Compare a scraped file with the site's own lists, its feed and the
  scraper's own log, and two files of the same scrape row for row.
- Lay out a scraping project so the build reruns from the saved pages.
- Fetch a page's past version from the Wayback Machine.
- Read a Wikipedia article's revision history from its API.

:::

## Three ways to get data from a website {#three-routes .smaller}

![](figures/15-scraping/D01-three-routes.png){width="90%" fig-align="center" fig-alt="Three lanes that all reach the Federal Reserve's data. Download a file: the H.15 interest-rate page offers its series as a CSV file. Request a feed: the address json/ne-press.json returns every press release as one data file in JSON. Scrape a page built for people: a program reads one statement page and picks the paragraphs out of its layout. Under each lane, what comes back: a file, a structured reply, the page's HTML."}

::: {style="font-size:0.78em"}

- **Web scraping**: a program reads pages built for people and copies
  chosen pieces into a table.
- **Feed or API**: a service that answers a program with data in a fixed
  structure.
- **HTML**: the text a web page is written in.

Scrape when the first two ways do not give what you need.

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

The **server** is the computer that holds the pages and answers requests.

:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
The feed holds 4,648 releases in the saved copy; your number will be
larger. The interest-rate page (H.15) offers its data files from its own
page.
:::

:::

## The Fed's policy statements, this session's data {#fed-statements .smaller}

::::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="46%"}

![](figures/15-scraping/S02-statement-20220615-top.png){fig-align="center" fig-alt="The top of one statement page on federalreserve.gov: the Press Release heading, the date June 15, 2022, the title Federal Reserve issues FOMC statement, and the first paragraphs of the statement."}

[The statement of 15 June 2022, as the site shows it.]{.source}

:::

::: {.column width="54%"}

::: {style="font-size:0.9em"}

The Federal Reserve is the US central bank. Its Federal Open Market
Committee (FOMC) sets the policy interest rate at eight scheduled meetings
a year. It publishes a written statement after each meeting. The
statements' text exists only on these pages.

This session collects every statement since 2006 into one file.

:::

:::

:::::

## Where to look before writing a scraper {#where-to-look .smaller}

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

Look in this order. A scraper is the last step.

| Look for | What it holds for the Fed's policy statements |
|:--------------------|:----------------------------------------------|
| 1. A dataset someone already built (a replication package, ICPSR, a vendor) | a paper's files stop at the end of its sample; this session needs every statement to the latest one |
| 2. A file to download on the site | interest rates as CSV files on the H.15 page; no statement text |
| 3. An API or feed | `json/ne-press.json`: every release's date, title and address; no text |
| 4. A licence or an agreement with the publisher | not needed: the Board's pages are public domain |
| 5. The pages themselves | the only place the text exists, so scrape |

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

ICPSR (the Inter-university Consortium for Political and Social Research)
is the largest US archive of social-science data; openICPSR holds many
journals' replication packages. The H.15 page is the Board's release of
selected interest rates.

:::

## Would you scrape Zillow's listings for a research project? {#hands}

::: {style="font-size:0.9em"}

Zillow lists homes for sale and for rent across the US.

**Hands.** Who would, and how?

:::

::: {.fragment style="font-size:0.78em"}

**Not with a scraper.**

- Its terms forbid "automated queries (including screen and database
  scraping, spiders, robots, crawlers ...)". Its robots.txt disallows
  `/homes/`. One polite request from R met a press-and-hold human check.
- The listing pages carry personal data: agents' names and phone numbers,
  photos of people's homes.
- The list on the last slide finds other routes: Zillow Research's CSV
  files (home values, rents, inventory), Zillow's transaction records
  (ZTRAX) through ICPSR, or listings licensed from an MLS or a data vendor.

:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
One or two call-outs on why, then click for the answer. The request was
to a page robots.txt allows (the research data page) and came back
"Access to this page has been denied" (October 2026). Part 3 explains
terms, robots.txt and the human check.

If a student raises the law: terms bind most clearly once you sign in. A
US court found that scraping public pages while logged out did not breach
Meta's terms (Meta Platforms v. Bright Data, N.D. Cal., 2024), and the hiQ
judgment turned on fake accounts. If a student raises the rental-housing
study coming up: a study like that goes through the IRB and the
university's counsel before any collection.
:::

:::

## Online prices scraped from 56 retailers, compared with their in-store prices {#cavallo .smaller}

Three papers built on scraped data: [Cavallo (AER, 2017)](https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.20160542).

::::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="56%"}

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.9em"}

- **Question.** Are the prices a retailer posts online the same as the
  prices in its stores?
- **What he did.** He wrote a scraping program for each of 56 large
  retailers in 10 countries. Hired workers scanned the same products in
  the stores and wrote down the shelf price. The program took the online
  price within a week.
- **Finding.** Prices were identical about 72 percent of the time. Online
  and in-store prices did not change on the same days, but changed about
  as often and by about as much.
- **Takeaway:** scraped prices can stand in for prices collected by hand
  once you have measured how often the two agree.

:::

:::

::: {.column width="44%"}

![](figures/15-scraping/D02-cavallo.png){width="100%" fig-align="center" fig-alt="One retailer's website goes through a scraper into a table of prices per product per day. Beside it a worker in the store scans the same product's barcode and writes down the shelf price. The two prices are compared."}

:::

:::::

## A million Chinese job ads from a crawler, coded for whether they ask for a man or a woman {#kuhn-shen .smaller}

[Kuhn & Shen (QJE, 2013)](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjs046)

::::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="56%"}

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.9em"}

- **Crawler**: a program that follows links from page to page and saves
  each one.
- **What they did.** They ran a crawler on Zhaopin.com, one of the
  largest Chinese online job boards, in four rounds of collection. It
  saved 1,051,706 ads. They coded whether each ad asked for a man, for a
  woman, or for neither.
- **Finding.** Ads that asked for one sex were common. They asked for
  women about as often as for men. They were much rarer in jobs that need
  more skill.
- **Takeaway:** a crawler turns a job board into data on what employers
  ask for, in their own words.

:::

:::

::: {.column width="44%"}

![](figures/15-scraping/D03-crawler.png){width="100%" fig-align="center" fig-alt="A crawler starts at a job board's listing page, follows each link to an ad, saves the ad, and moves to the next listing page. The saved ads become rows of a table: the job, the employer, and whether the ad asks for a man or a woman."}

:::

:::::

## Discrimination in rental housing, measured with inquiries to scraped listings {#christensen .smaller}

[Christensen & Timmins (QJE, 2023)](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjad029)

::::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="56%"}

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.88em"}

- **Context.** US law (the Fair Housing Act) bans discrimination by race
  in renting a home.
- **What they did.** A program collected every three-bedroom,
  two-bathroom rental listing on a major online platform in five US
  metropolitan areas, with each neighbourhood's amenities and pollution.
  It then sent each listing inquiries from fictitious renters whose names
  signal race or ethnicity. The replies are the data.
- **Finding.** Discrimination cost African American renters the
  equivalent of 4.4 percent of annual income, and Hispanic/Latinx renters
  3.5 percent.
- **Takeaway:** scraping supplied the sample of homes and each home's
  neighbourhood data. The inquiries supplied the outcome.

:::

:::

::: {.column width="44%"}

![](figures/15-scraping/D04-inquiries.png){width="100%" fig-align="center" fig-alt="Rental listings go through a scraper into a table of homes with their neighbourhood's amenities and pollution. From the table, inquiries go out to each listing from renters with different names, and the replies come back and are recorded."}

:::

## The Fed's meeting calendar {#calendar .smaller}

![](figures/15-scraping/S01-calendar-2025-jan-mar.png){fig-align="center" fig-alt="The top of the 2025 panel of the Federal Reserve's meeting calendar: the heading 2025 FOMC Meetings, then one row per meeting with the month, the dates, links to the statement as PDF and HTML, the implementation note, the press conference, the projection materials and the minutes."}

::: {style="font-size:0.78em"}

- The FOMC (the Fed's policy committee) issues a statement on the last
  day of each meeting.
- One page, [federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomccalendars.htm](https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomccalendars.htm),
  lists 2021 to 2027: one panel (box) per year, one row per meeting.
- Each row links the statement (PDF and HTML), an implementation note
  (the technical instructions that go with the decision), the press
  conference and the minutes (the written record of the meeting).
- Each year from 2006 to 2020 has its own page. Each statement has its
  own page.

:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
Unscheduled calls, and votes taken in writing (notation votes), happen in
crises; the 2025 panel's last row is one, "August 22 (notation vote)".
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

## The statements file this session builds {#statements-file .smaller}

```{r}
#| label: statements-file
#| filename: "R Console, in the 15-scraping folder; reads fomc_statements.csv, the statements file (built from cache/ by build_statements.R)"
ours <- read.csv("fomc_statements.csv")                  # ours: the statements file
dim(ours)
ours[c(1, nrow(ours)), c("date", "words", "scheduled")]  # the first and the last row
```

::: {style="font-size:0.78em"}

- **Press release**: one page in the Fed's press-release section.
- **Policy statement**: the release that announces the committee's rate
  decision after a meeting or a call. From here on, "statement" means
  policy statement. The file leaves out the site's other releases:
  implementation notes, the longer-run-goals statement, lending
  announcements.
- One row per statement, 31 January 2006 to 16 September 2026. The file stops
  at the pages saved on 18 October 2026; the live site adds a statement
  after each meeting.
- Columns: `date`, `url`, `words`, `text`, `scheduled`. `scheduled` is
  TRUE after a scheduled meeting and FALSE after an unscheduled call or a
  notation vote (a vote taken in writing).

:::

[Every page used today was saved into `cache/` on 18 October 2026, in the
268 requests that built it. `SOURCE.txt` lists every file.]{.source}

:::

## Elements, tags, classes, ids and attributes in HTML {#html .smaller}

![](figures/15-scraping/D05-html-row.png){width="90%" fig-align="center" fig-alt="Left, the HTML of the January 2024 calendar row, trimmed to ten lines: a div with class row fomc-meeting, inside it a div with class fomc-meeting__month holding January in bold, a div with class fomc-meeting__date holding 30-31, and a div with the Statement links: PDF, HTML and Implementation Note, each an a tag with an href. Right, the same row as the browser draws it. Four arrows join the month, the dates, the HTML link and the Implementation Note link to their lines of HTML."}

::: {style="font-size:0.78em"}

- **Element**: one labelled piece of the page (a heading, a link, a box).
- **Tag**: the label in angle brackets (`div`, `a`, `strong`).
- **Class**: a name the site gives to elements of one kind
  (`fomc-meeting`); many elements share it.
- **Id**: a name given to one element only. On the Fed's pages `article`
  is the main text box, on the calendar and on each statement.
- **Attribute**: a named value inside a tag; a link's address is its
  `href`.

:::

## Finding an element with the browser inspector {#inspector .smaller}

![](figures/15-scraping/S04-inspector-row.png){width="88%" fig-align="center" fig-alt="The browser inspector with the HTML of a calendar row expanded: a div with class row fomc-meeting, and inside it the month, the dates and the Statement links, with the HTML link to monetary20240131a.htm highlighted."}

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

**Browser inspector**: the window that shows the HTML behind whatever you
point at. Right-click a meeting date on the live page, choose
**Inspect**, and read the class names on the highlighted line and on the
lines inside it.

**View Source** (right-click, View Page Source) shows the file the server
sent; that is what R reads. Safari needs "Show features for web
developers" turned on in its Advanced settings first.

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

Inspect shows the page after its scripts ran, and View Source shows the
file as the server sent it. If the two differ, the page is dynamic: its
scripts fetched the content after the page loaded, and `read_html()`
gets the file without that content.

:::

## Picking out elements with CSS selectors {#selectors .smaller}

::: {style="font-size:0.85em"}

**CSS selector**: a short pattern that names elements. The table shows
the kinds used today and how many elements each picks out of the saved
calendar.

| Selector | Picks | Count |
|:---------------|:-----------------------------|-----:|
| `p` | every paragraph (by tag) | 50 |
| `.fomc-meeting` | every element with class `fomc-meeting` | 57 |
| `#article` | the one element with id `article` | 1 |
| `#article p` | paragraphs inside that element | 4 |
| `a[href*='pressreleases/monetary']` | links whose address contains this text | 100 |
| `a[href$='a.htm']` | links whose address ends in `a.htm` | 53 |

`.fomc-meeting` matches the class `fomc-meeting` exactly, not
`fomc-meeting__month`. On a statement page, `#article p` returns the
statement's own paragraphs (Exercise 2).

:::

## Reading the saved calendar with `read_html()` {#read-html .smaller}

```{r}
#| label: read-html
#| filename: "R Console, in the 15-scraping folder; needs rvest; reads cache/fomccalendars.htm; no network"
# install.packages(c("rvest", "httr2", "jsonlite"))   # once
library(rvest)
cal    <- read_html("cache/fomccalendars.htm")       # the calendar as saved
panels <- html_elements(cal, ".panel-default")       # one panel per year
length(panels)
titles <- html_text2(html_element(panels, "h4"))     # the first h4 (a heading) inside each panel
titles
```

::: {style="font-size:0.78em"}

- `read_html()` reads a file or an address into R.
- `html_elements()` returns every match.
- `html_element()` returns the first match inside each element.
- `html_text2()` returns the text as the browser shows it.
- The order is the page's: 2026 first, 2027 last.

:::

## The 2024 meeting rows as text {#rows-2024 .smaller}

```{r}
#| label: rows-2024
#| filename: "R Console; needs panels and titles from the previous step"
p2024 <- panels[titles == "2024 FOMC Meetings"]
rows  <- html_elements(p2024, ".fomc-meeting")
length(rows)
data.frame(month = html_text2(html_element(rows, ".fomc-meeting__month")),
           dates = html_text2(html_element(rows, ".fomc-meeting__date")))
```

::: {style="font-size:0.78em"}

The eight rows are the eight scheduled meetings of a year. The asterisk
marks a meeting that also publishes the members' economic projections
(the page's footnote: "Meeting associated with a Summary of Economic
Projections").

:::

## The links in one row, with `html_attr()` {#html-attr .smaller}

```{r}
#| label: html-attr
#| filename: "R Console; needs rows"
links <- html_elements(rows[1], "a")                 # the links in the January row
data.frame(text = substr(html_text2(links), 1, 24),  # substr(): the first 24 characters
           file = basename(html_attr(links, "href")))  # basename(): the file name at the end of the address
```

::: {style="font-size:0.78em"}

- `html_attr()` returns one attribute of each element; `href` is the
  link's address. The addresses start with `/`: they are relative, and
  the site's name goes in front when you fetch them.
- The Fed publishes each statement as a press release, a page under
  `/newsevents/pressreleases/`. This row has three such links (rows 2, 3
  and 5); only row 2 is the statement,
  `/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20240131a.htm`.
- The next slide counts the statement links by the end of the address
  and by the link text.

:::

## Counting the calendar's statement links three ways {#three-counts .smaller}

```{r}
#| label: three-counts
#| filename: "R Console; needs cal"
# both selectors start with .fomc-meeting: 6 more a.htm links sit outside the rows
a1 <- html_elements(cal, ".fomc-meeting a[href*='pressreleases/monetary']")  # address contains this
a2 <- html_elements(cal, ".fomc-meeting a[href$='a.htm']")                   # address ends in a.htm
c(contains = length(a1), ends_a = length(a2),
  text_HTML = sum(html_text2(a1) == "HTML"))     # sum() counts the TRUEs
```

::: {style="font-size:0.78em"}

- The calendar holds 46 statements: 57 rows, minus 10 meetings not yet
  held by the day the page was saved, minus one row that is not a
  meeting.
- `contains`, 100: every press-release link in the rows (46 statements,
  46 implementation notes, 6 longer-run-goals statements, 2 balance-sheet
  plans).
- `ends_a`, 47: one more than the statements. Exercise 1 finds the row
  that holds it.
- `text_HTML`, 46: the links named HTML are the statements. Keep this
  count.

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

## Reading an HTML table with `html_table()` {#html-table .smaller}

::: {style="font-size:0.78em"}

Some pages hold their data in a `<table>`. The calendar does not, so this
example uses Wikipedia's table of Fed chairs, saved as
`cache/wiki_fed_chairs.htm` (text CC BY-SA).

:::

```{r}
#| label: html-table
#| filename: "R Console, in the 15-scraping folder; needs rvest; reads cache/wiki_fed_chairs.htm"
wiki   <- read_html("cache/wiki_fed_chairs.htm")
tbl    <- html_element(wiki, "table.wikitable")      # the first table of that class
chairs <- as.data.frame(html_table(tbl))             # as.data.frame(): a plain data frame print
dim(chairs)
unlist(chairs[1, 4:5])          # the header spans two rows; its second row arrives as data
chairs <- chairs[-1, ]                               # drop it
names(chairs) <- c("no", "portrait", "name", "start", "end", "duration", "appointer", "experience", "education")
tail(chairs[, c("no", "name", "start", "end")], 3)
```

::: {style="font-size:0.72em"}

- `html_table()` turns one `<table>` into a data frame.
- This table has a two-row header. Its second header row arrives as data
  row 1: drop it and name the columns yourself.
- Footnote markers (`[h]`) and "(born 1953)" stay inside the cells. That
  cleaning is yours.

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

![The table as the page shows it: a two-row header (Term spans Start and End) and cells that span rows (one appointer for two chairs), which is why the data frame needs cleaning.](figures/15-scraping/S07-wiki-chairs-table-top.png){fig-alt="The top of the Wikipedia table of Federal Reserve chairs: a header row with Name, Term split into Start and End, Duration, Appointer, Experience and Education, then the first four chairs with portraits; Woodrow Wilson's cell spans two rows."}

## Exercise 1 {#exercise-1 .smaller}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Exercise

::: {style="font-size:1.4em"}

```{r}
#| label: exercise-1
#| exercise: true
#| script: "Exercise 1 (5 minutes)"
#| eval: false
# Exercise 1 (5 minutes). R Console, in the 15-scraping folder; needs rvest.
# No network. If you do not have cal, panels and titles yet, run these three:
#   cal    <- read_html("cache/fomccalendars.htm")
#   panels <- html_elements(cal, ".panel-default")
#   titles <- html_text2(html_element(panels, "h4"))
#
# 1. Keep the panel titled "2025 FOMC Meetings".
# 2. Select its .fomc-meeting rows and count them with length().
# 3. Print each row's month (.fomc-meeting__month) and dates
#    (.fomc-meeting__date) in one data frame.
# 4. Find the row that is not a meeting.
#
# Two answers to compare with the room: the number of rows, and
# which row is not a meeting.
```

:::

### Solution

```{r}
#| label: exercise-1-solution
#| purl: false
#| filename: "R Console; needs panels and titles"
p2025 <- panels[titles == "2025 FOMC Meetings"]
rows  <- html_elements(p2025, ".fomc-meeting")
length(rows)
data.frame(month = html_text2(html_element(rows, ".fomc-meeting__month")),
           dates = html_text2(html_element(rows, ".fomc-meeting__date")))
```

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

**Nine rows. Row 6, "August 22 (notation vote)", is a decision taken in
writing without a meeting. Its release approved updates to the
committee's Statement on Longer-Run Goals, so it is not a policy
statement; its link ends in `a.htm`, which is why the count before was 47
and not 46.**

:::

:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
Uses only the functions of the last four slides. This is the one year
where a count of rows and a count of policy statements differ. Debrief by
call-out: who got nine?
:::

## A static page and a dynamic one {#dynamic .smaller}

::: {style="font-size:0.85em"}

- **Static page**: the HTML the server sends is the page you see.
- **Dynamic page**: the server sends an empty layout plus scripts. In a
  browser the scripts fetch the content after the page loads.
  `read_html()` runs no scripts, so it gets the empty layout.
- **Example**: the Fed's press-release list page. Its saved HTML is 85 KB
  and contains "FOMC statement" zero times; the browser shows hundreds of
  release titles.
- **The test**: View Source, then search for a title you can see on the
  page. If the source does not contain it, the page is dynamic. In R:
  `sum(grepl("FOMC statement", readLines("cache/pressreleases.htm")))`
  returns 0.

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

![The same page as the browser draws it: a list of releases that the HTML the server sends does not contain.](figures/15-scraping/S03-pressreleases-list.png){fig-alt="The Federal Reserve's press-release list page in a browser: a date filter, type checkboxes, and the first releases listed by date."}

:::

## Three ways to read a dynamic page {#dynamic-remedies .smaller}

![](figures/15-scraping/S05-network.png){width="78%" fig-align="center" fig-alt="The inspector's Network tab open on the Federal Reserve's press-release list page, with the search box set to ne-press: one request for json/ne-press.json, the file the page's scripts load to fill the list."}

[The inspector's Network tab on the Fed's press-release list page, with
the search box set to ne-press: the page's script requests
json/ne-press.json.]{.source}

::: {style="font-size:0.78em"}

1. Request the file the page loads. Find it in the inspector's Network
   tab; here `json/ne-press.json`, read on the next slide.
2. Right-click that request and choose Copy as cURL (a command-line
   program for web requests). `curl_translate()` from httr2 turns the
   copied text into the same request in R.
3. A **headless browser**, a browser run by a program with no window:
   `read_html_live()` in rvest, with the chromote package and Chrome.
   Use it when no clean file shows.

:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
The feed's address is assembled by the page's script, so it is not in the
HTML or in the main script file; the Network tab (filtered to Fetch/XHR)
is where it shows.
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

In more detail: open the inspector, choose the Network tab, filter to
Fetch/XHR, and reload the page; the requests the page's scripts make
appear with their addresses. When a site offers a JSON endpoint the page
itself calls, request that endpoint with the same politeness as a page.
`read_html_live()` opens a real browser in the background through the
chromote package, so install chromote and have Chrome on the computer. It
is slower than reading a saved file, and the site's terms apply to it as
to any program.

:::

## Reading the feed the page loads with `fromJSON()` {#feed .smaller}

```{r}
#| label: feed
#| warning: false
#| filename: "R Console, in the 15-scraping folder; needs jsonlite; reads cache/ne-press.json (live address below)"
library(jsonlite)
feed <- fromJSON("cache/ne-press.json")     # warns about a byte-order mark (three invisible bytes); harmless
dim(feed)
fs <- feed[grepl("FOMC statement", feed$t), ]   # titles that contain the phrase; t is the title column
nrow(fs)
table(fs$t)[c("Federal Reserve issues FOMC statement", "FOMC statement")]   # the two common titles
```

::: {style="font-size:0.75em"}

- **JSON**: a plain-text format for data. `fromJSON()` turns the feed
  into a data frame of 4,648 releases: `d` is the date, `t` the title,
  `l` the link. Live address: `federalreserve.gov/json/ne-press.json`.
- The feed gives every release's address in one request. The statement
  text still lives on each page.
- 179 titles contain "FOMC statement": 123 and 46 with the two common
  titles, 10 with longer ones. The statements file has 171 rows; Part 5
  explains the difference.
- A PDF or a CSV is fetched and saved like a page, as the bytes the
  server sent. Only the reader changes: pdftools for a PDF, `read.csv()`
  for a CSV.

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

The feed has seven columns: `d` the date, `t` the title (HTML-escaped:
`&` written as `&amp;`), `pt` the type, `l` the link, and three more. The
ten longer titles name the dollar swap lines, the longer-run goals and a
change of release times.

:::

## Six routes to every page on a site {#six-routes .smaller}

::: {style="font-size:0.72em"}

| Route | Example | When it fits | Load on the server |
|:----------|:-----------------------|:------------|:-----------|
| The site's feed or API | `ne-press.json`, 4,648 releases in one request | the site offers one | one request |
| An index page with links | the calendar: 57 rows, 100 release links | a list page exists | one page |
| The sitemap | `bls.gov/sitemap.xml`, a sitemap index | robots.txt names one | one request per sitemap file |
| Pagination | one year page per year; `?page=2` elsewhere | the address carries the page number | one request per page |
| A crawler that follows every link | the job board in [Kuhn & Shen (QJE, 2013)](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjs046) | no list exists | the heaviest; robots.txt governs it |
| Bought data | about 100 million postings a vendor crawled, in [Hershbein & Kahn (AER, 2018)](https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.20161570) | the licence fits your use | none |

**Sitemap**: an XML file listing a site's pages for search engines; a
sitemap index lists other sitemaps.

:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
The BLS index opens with sitemap-home.xml, advisory/sitemap-advisory.xml,
air/sitemap-air.xml, and answers 403 without a contact address. The
Internet Archive's listing also holds pages the site has since removed
(Part 7). Whatever the route, write down what you believe the full list
is and compare your count with it.
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

![The BLS sitemap index: one entry per section of the site, each pointing to a sitemap of its own.](figures/15-scraping/S05-bls-sitemap.png){fig-alt="An XML sitemap index from bls.gov listing sitemap files for each section of the site."}

Hershbein and Kahn found that skill requirements in postings rose more in
US metropolitan areas hit harder by the 2008 recession and stayed higher.
Their postings came from Burning Glass Technologies, through a special
agreement, for 2007 and 2010 to 2015.

:::

- Terms of use, copyright, robots.txt, personal data

## Terms of use set a site's rules for visitors {#terms .smaller}

::: {style="font-size:0.9em"}

**Terms of use**: the legal rules a site sets for visitors. Using the site
means accepting them. They may forbid automated copying. Look for footer
links named Terms, Legal, Website Policies or Disclaimer.

- **Zillow**, a US website that lists homes for sale and rent, forbids
  "automated queries (including screen and database scraping, spiders,
  robots, crawlers ...)".
- **The Fed** keeps its terms on its
  [Disclaimer page](https://www.federalreserve.gov/disclaimer.htm). Its
  copyright section is on the next slide.

:::

## Copyright and facts {#copyright .smaller}

![](figures/15-scraping/S01-disclaimer-public-domain.png){fig-align="center" fig-alt="The Copyright/trademark section of the Federal Reserve Board's disclaimer page: unless otherwise indicated, information on the Board's website is in the public domain and may be copied and distributed without permission; please cite the Board as the source. Material identified as non-Board, such as photos and graphics, keeps its owner's permission."}

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

- **Copyright**: the owner's right to control copies of a text, image or
  recording.
- **Public domain**: nobody holds the copyright, so anyone may copy it.
  The Federal Reserve Board (the Board), which runs federalreserve.gov,
  puts its own material there (above). Cite the Board.
- **Facts**: in the US, copyright does not cover them. A telephone
  directory's names and numbers may be copied by anyone (US Supreme
  Court, Feist v. Rural, 1991). Prices, dates and vote counts are facts.
- The wording of a text is covered, unless it is public domain or
  **licensed** (released under terms that allow copying).

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

Outside the US, the European Union also protects a database built with
substantial investment, apart from copyright (the database right,
Directive 96/9/EC, article 7), even when it holds only facts. For a
project: collect the facts; republishing scraped full texts, for example
in a replication package, needs the text to be public domain (the Fed) or
licensed (Wikipedia: CC BY-SA, with attribution). The EU's copyright
directive of 2019 (Directive 2019/790) gives research organisations an
exception for text and data mining of material they may lawfully access
(article 3; article 4 covers other uses).

Zillow's terms of use, on the clause about automated access: users may
"copy information from the Services without the aid of any automated
processes and only as necessary for your personal use" and may not
"conduct automated queries (including screen and database scraping,
spiders, robots, crawlers, bypassing 'captcha' or similar precautions, or
any other automated activity with the purpose of obtaining information
from the Services)".

**hiQ Labs v. LinkedIn.** hiQ, an analytics firm, scraped public LinkedIn
profiles to sell reports to employers. An appeals court held in April
2022 that hiQ raised serious questions whether scraping public pages is
access "without authorization" under the US anti-hacking law (the CFAA).
The trial court found in November 2022 that hiQ had breached LinkedIn's
User Agreement, which bans scraping; a consent judgment followed in
December 2022 (hiQ to stop scraping and destroy the data), and it
recorded a CFAA violation for hiQ's access to password-protected pages
through fake accounts. Public pages can be off-limits under a site's
terms, and pages behind a login are off-limits under the law.

:::

## robots.txt lists the paths a site asks programs to skip {#robots .smaller}

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

**robots.txt**: a plain-text file at a site's main address
(`/robots.txt`) that tells programs which paths to stay out of. The
server (the computer that holds the pages) does not enforce it. A polite
scraper follows it.

- **federalreserve.gov/robots.txt** does not exist. The server answers
  with **status code** 404, not found (the status code is the three-digit
  number at the top of every reply). The standard for robots.txt
  (RFC 9309) treats a 404 as no restriction.
- **zillow.com/robots.txt**, 328 lines; the lines that matter:

:::

```{.default filename="zillow.com/robots.txt as read on 18 October 2026, 6 of its 328 lines; the comments after a line are my notes"}
# Access to and use of Zillow.com is governed by our Terms of Use. See https://www.zillow.com/corp/Terms.htm
User-agent: *                   # line 3: every program
Allow: /homes/for_sale/$        # one of 64 Allow lines: the listing-index pages
Disallow: /homes/               # line 50, one of 212 Disallow lines: the listings
Crawl-delay: 1                  # line 302, in a block for one named crawler
Sitemap: https://www.zillow.com/xml/indexes/us/static.xml.gz   # 15 Sitemap lines
```

::: {style="font-size:0.78em"}

- `User-agent`: the name a program sends with each request. A block (the
  lines that follow) applies to the programs named; `*` means every
  program.
- `Disallow`: paths to skip (a path is the part of an address after the
  site name).
- `Allow`: exceptions to a Disallow (`$` means the address ends there).
- `Crawl-delay`: seconds to wait between requests; not in the standard,
  but some sites write it.
- `Sitemap`: where the site lists the pages it wants found (Part 2).

:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
The file forbids the listing pages a researcher would want; Part 1's hands question drew on it. Eleven crawlers are named in later blocks:
Amazonbot, for one, is disallowed everywhere except guides and blog
pages. The three social-media crawlers at lines 261 to 265 form their
own group with two Allow lines; the four at lines 304 to 309 are fully
disallowed. The Fed's sitemap.xml answers 404 as well. Measured 18
October 2026.
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

RFC 9309, section 2.3.1.3: "If a server status code indicates that the
robots.txt file is unavailable to the crawler, then the crawler MAY
access any resources on the server." The RFC defines no `Crawl-delay`
field and lists `Sitemap` as a record outside the protocol.

:::

## Personal data on the pages you scrape {#personal-data .smaller}

![](figures/15-scraping/S02-transcript-reporter.png){fig-align="center" fig-alt="Three lines of a press-conference transcript: a reporter gives her name and her newspaper, then asks the chair about interest rates."}

[From a Fed press-conference transcript (a PDF on federalreserve.gov):
the reporter's name and outlet.]{.source}

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.8em"}

- **Personal data**: information that identifies a living person: a name,
  a photo, an address, an email, an IP address.
- **On the Fed's site.** The statements name the voting members. They act
  in public roles, so naming them raises no privacy issue. The
  press-conference transcripts name each reporter and outlet (above).
- **For research.**
  - Collect only the fields you need.
  - Research on identifiable people goes to the IRB (the university board
    that approves research on people) before you collect.
  - The EU's data-protection law (GDPR) covers personal data on public
    pages too, and counts an IP address.

:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
The Wikipedia request later today leaves the editor's name out. GDPR:
article 4(1) defines personal data; recital 30 names IP addresses and
cookie identifiers.
:::

:::

## Identifying yourself with a user agent {#user-agent .smaller}

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

- **User agent**: the name a program sends with every request. Put who
  you are and how to reach you in it. A robots.txt `User-agent` line
  matches this name.
- Status codes: 200 means OK, 403 means forbidden.
- Three requests to bls.gov (the US Bureau of Labor Statistics) with
  httr2, the R package that sends requests; one request per row.

| User agent sent | Status code |
|:--|:--|
| no user agent set (httr2 sends its own name) | 403 Forbidden, an "Access Denied" page |
| `AEM 6850 class exercise` (a name, no email) | 403 Forbidden |
| `AEM 6850 class exercise; <your netid>@cornell.edu` | 200 OK, the page |

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

The site's [policy](https://www.bls.gov/bls/pss.htm): "BLS also reserves
the right to block robots that do not contain information that can be
used to contact the owner. Blocking may occur in real time."

:::

```{r}
#| label: bls
#| eval: false
#| purl: false
#| filename: "R Console; needs internet and httr2; two requests; run after class (Practice 6), not in the room"
library(httr2)
req <- request("https://www.bls.gov/cpi/")
req <- req_error(req, is_error = function(resp) FALSE)   # a 403 comes back as a reply, not an R error
resp_status(req_perform(req))                            # httr2's default user agent
#> [1] 403
req <- req_user_agent(req, "AEM 6850 class exercise; <your netid>@cornell.edu")
resp_status(req_perform(req))
#> [1] 200
```

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
The 403 page's own words: "Automated retrieval programs (commonly called
robots or bots) can cause delays and interfere with other customers'
timely access to information. Therefore, bot activity that doesn't
conform to BLS usage policy is prohibited." Wikimedia's policy asks for a
contact address as well (Part 7). The policy page itself answers 403 to a
user agent without an email. Measured 18 October 2026.
:::

:::

## What the server's reply means, and what to do {#status-codes .smaller}

::: {style="font-size:0.82em"}

| Status code | Meaning | What to do | Seen in this session |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| 200 | it worked | go on; save the page | all 268 requests that built `cache/` |
| 301, 302 | the address moved | httr2 follows it; save the final address | 46 of them, old addresses on the 2006 to 2010 year pages |
| 403 | forbidden | stop; read the site's policy; identify yourself | bls.gov, with no email in the user agent |
| 404 | no such page | record it; do not retry | federalreserve.gov/robots.txt |
| 429 | too many requests | wait, then retry with a longer pause each time | none, at one request a second |
| 500 and above | the server failed | retry later | none |

A 200 can still be the wrong page: a consent page, a login page or an
error page. Before saving, test for a phrase the real page must contain,
such as "FOMC statement" in its title.

:::

::: {style="font-size:0.72em"}

- **Rate limit**: the most requests a site accepts from one IP address
  (the number that identifies a computer on the network) per minute or
  hour. Above it the reply is 429, often with a `Retry-After`
  line saying how long to wait.
- **Backoff**: waiting longer after each failure. `req_retry()` reads
  `Retry-After` and backs off.

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

`Retry-After` sits in the reply's header, the metadata that comes with
every reply.

:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
The prep scrape's 268 requests and the agent's 191, at one per second,
all returned 200. Keep every request's status in a log; the log is how
you know which pages you still owe. The redirects were the old
/press/monetary/ addresses on the 2006 to 2010 year pages.
:::

:::

## What to do at a CAPTCHA and at a login wall {#captcha-login}

![](figures/15-scraping/D06-captcha-login.png){.r-stretch fig-align="center" fig-alt="Two columns. Left, a CAPTCHA: a test that a person is at the keyboard, such as distorted letters or picking pictures. It is the site's refusal to programs: stop, slow down, put your name and address in the user agent, then ask the site for access or for its feed. Do not have a program solve it. Right, a login wall: the page shows only after you sign in. It is a terms question: the terms you accepted say what a program may copy. Where they allow it, use your own credentials in your own session, at the rate a person would read. Pages behind your login are also where an AI browser agent fits."}

::: {style="font-size:0.66em"}

Address spoofing and proxy rotation hide who is asking. Sites ban the
scrapers that use them, and this course does not teach them.

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

Address spoofing is pretending the request comes from another computer;
proxy rotation is sending requests through many borrowed addresses.

A logged-in session in R, where the terms allow it: `req_cookie_preserve()`
keeps the cookies a site sets across requests, and a browser's "Copy as
cURL" on a request made while signed in, passed through
`curl_translate()`, reproduces that request in httr2 with your cookie. The
cookie is a credential: it never goes in a script, a repository or a
chat. Zillow's terms name "bypassing 'captcha' or similar precautions"
among forbidden automated activity, and the hiQ consent judgment recorded
a violation of the US anti-hacking law for reaching password-protected
pages through fake accounts.

:::

## `fetch_page()` sends one polite request and saves the reply {#fetch-page .smaller}

```{r}
#| label: fetch-page
#| filename: "R Console, in the 15-scraping folder; needs httr2; defines fetch_page() and fetches nothing yet"
# the same function ships as fetch_page.R: source("fetch_page.R")
library(httr2)
fetch_page <- function(url, file, ua) {
  if (file.exists(file)) return("already saved")          # never fetch a page twice
  req  <- request(url)
  req  <- req_user_agent(req, ua)                         # who you are and how to reach you
  req  <- req_retry(req, max_tries = 4)                   # a 429 or 503: wait (Retry-After if given), try again
  req  <- req_error(req, is_error = function(resp) FALSE) # a 403 or 404 comes back as a reply, not an R error
  resp <- req_perform(req)
  if (resp_status(resp) == 200) writeBin(resp_body_raw(resp), file)   # the bytes exactly as sent
  write(paste(url, file, format(Sys.time()), resp_status(resp), sep = ","),
        "mine/fetch_log.csv", append = TRUE)              # one log row per request, failures included
  Sys.sleep(1)                                            # one request a second
  resp_status(resp)
}
```

## `fetch_page()` writes to `mine/` and to a fetch log {#fetch-page-files .smaller}

```{r}
#| label: fetch-page-files
#| filename: "R Console, in the 15-scraping folder; run once before the first fetch_page() call"
dir.create("mine", showWarnings = FALSE)                  # your own fetches go here; cache/ stays as shipped
if (!file.exists("mine/fetch_log.csv")) writeLines("url,file,time,status", "mine/fetch_log.csv")
```

::: {style="font-size:0.85em"}

- **Cache**: the saved copies on disk. A rerun reads them instead of
  asking the server again.
- **Raw bytes**: the reply exactly as the server sent it. `writeBin()`
  keeps them; `writeLines()` would rewrite the text and could change
  characters.
- **Fetch log**: one row per request (url, file, time, status). Read it
  back with `read.csv("mine/fetch_log.csv")`.
- **The pause**: every laptop in the room sends from Cornell's network,
  which a site may count as one visitor. `Sys.sleep(1)` keeps each
  request slow.

:::

## Exercise 2 {#exercise-2 .smaller}

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

Fetch one statement page yourself with `fetch_page()`, then read its
paragraphs with `read_html()` and `#article p` (a statement page keeps
its text in the same `#article` box as the calendar). The page is the
statement of 15 June 2022.

:::

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Exercise

::: {style="font-size:1.1em"}

```{r}
#| label: exercise-2
#| exercise: true
#| script: "Exercise 2 (5 minutes)"
#| eval: false
# Exercise 2 (5 minutes). R Console, in the 15-scraping folder; needs
# fetch_page(): run source("fetch_page.R") if it is not defined yet. One
# live request. Step 2's two lines are long: copy them from fetch_page.R.
#
# 1. Put your own address in the user agent:
#    ua <- "AEM 6850 student; <your netid>@cornell.edu"
# 2. Fetch the 15 June 2022 statement into mine/:
#    fetch_page("https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20220615a.htm",
#               "mine/monetary20220615a.htm", ua)
#    No network? file.copy("cache/monetary20220615a.htm", "mine/"), then the same line.
# 3. Read the saved file with read_html() and select "#article p".
# 4. Count the paragraphs with length(); print them with html_text2().
#
# Two answers to compare with the room: the number of paragraphs, and
# which paragraph names the member who voted against the decision.
```

:::

### Solution

```{r}
#| label: exercise-2-solution
#| purl: false
#| eval: false
#| filename: "R Console; needs fetch_page() and ua. Output recorded when the exercise was tested; the shipped copy gives the same eight paragraphs"
fetch_page("https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20220615a.htm",
           "mine/monetary20220615a.htm", ua)
#> [1] 200
s  <- read_html("mine/monetary20220615a.htm")
ps <- html_text2(html_elements(s, "#article p"))
length(ps)
#> [1] 8
substr(ps, 1, 60)                       # substr(): the first 60 characters of each paragraph
#> [1] "June 15, 2022"
#> [2] "For release at 2:00 p.m. EDT"
#> [3] "Overall economic activity appears to have picked up after ed"
#> [4] "The invasion of Ukraine by Russia is causing tremendous huma"
#> [5] "The Committee seeks to achieve maximum employment and inflat"
#> [6] "In assessing the appropriate stance of monetary policy, the "
#> [7] "Voting for the monetary policy action were Jerome H. Powell,"
#> [8] "Implementation Note issued June 15, 2022"
```

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

**Eight paragraphs. Three are not statement text: the date line, "For
release at 2:00 p.m. EDT", and the last one, a link to the implementation
note. The vote is paragraph 7: Esther L. George voted against, preferring
an increase of 0.5 percentage point.**

:::

:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
That statement raised the federal funds rate (the overnight rate between
banks) to 1.5 to 1.75 percent. Debrief by call-out: run step 2 again and
it returns "already saved" at once; read.csv("mine/fetch_log.csv") shows one row, status 200; open the
page in the browser: the same paragraphs, with the site's header and the
note link around them. One request per laptop leaves the room, each with
a user agent and a one-second pause; the runs that built cache/ and the
agent's run saw no 429 at one per second, and req_retry() handles one if
it comes. Older
statements carry other extras: the January 2006 statement opens with "For
immediate release" and ends with the Board's discount-rate action.
:::

:::

## Reading the fifteen year pages, 2006 to 2020, in a loop {#year-loop .smaller}

::: {style="font-size:0.78em"}

The calendar covers 2021 to 2027. Each year from 2006 to 2020 has its own
page. The loop reads all fifteen with `fetch_page()`.

:::

```{r}
#| label: year-loop
#| filename: "R Console, in the 15-scraping folder; needs rvest, httr2 and fetch_page(); the year pages are in cache/, so nothing is fetched"
ua  <- "AEM 6850 student; <your netid>@cornell.edu"       # any name with your address works
out <- data.frame()
for (y in 2006:2020) {
  url  <- sprintf("https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomchistorical%d.htm", y)
  file <- sprintf("cache/fomchistorical%d.htm", y)
  fetch_page(url, file, ua)                               # returns "already saved": the file is in cache/
  page <- read_html(file)
  h5   <- html_text2(html_elements(page, ".panel-default h5"))   # one heading per meeting or call
  a    <- html_elements(page, "a")                        # every link; here every Statement link sits inside a panel
  out  <- rbind(out, data.frame(year = y, listed = length(h5),
                                statements = sum(html_text2(a) == "Statement")))
}
```

::: {style="font-size:0.78em"}

- **Pagination**: a list split across pages that a scraper visits in
  turn. Here the year is in the address, and `sprintf("%d")` fills it in.
- Each page lists its meetings and calls as panels with an `h5` heading,
  such as "January 30-31 Meeting - 2007" or "August 10 Conference Call -
  2007". The statement is the link named Statement. Output on the next
  slide.

:::

## The year pages list 145 entries and 129 statements {#year-counts .smaller}

```{r}
#| label: year-counts
#| filename: "R Console; needs out from the loop"
colSums(out[, c("listed", "statements")])
print(out[out$listed != out$statements, ], row.names = FALSE)   # the eight years that differ
```

::: {style="font-size:0.78em"}

- 145 entries (one `h5` heading each) and 129 links named Statement.
- In the seven years not printed, every entry issued a statement: eight a
  year, nine in 2019 (one unscheduled entry).
- The extra entries are conference calls (2007 to 2011), unscheduled
  entries (2013, 2014, 2020), four notation votes and one cancelled
  meeting (2020).
- Some calls issued a statement and some did not: 2009's three issued
  none, 2008's six issued three.

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

The full table:

```{r}

#| purl: false
print(out, row.names = FALSE)
```

The conference calls per year: 2007: 3, 2008: 6, 2009: 3, 2010: 2, 2011:
2. Four of the 129 links named Statement lead to liquidity or
implementation releases (August 2007, March 2008, May 2010, October
2019); Part 5 meets them.

:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
Calls per year: 2007: 3, 2008: 6, 2009: 3, 2010: 2, 2011: 2. The 2020
page: seven scheduled meetings held, the March 17-18 meeting cancelled,
two unscheduled meetings and four notation votes; ten statements.

## Two pitfalls in the statement addresses on the year pages {#address-forms .smaller}

```{r}
#| label: address-forms
#| filename: "R Console; needs rvest; reads cache/fomchistorical2008.htm"
p08  <- read_html("cache/fomchistorical2008.htm")
a08  <- html_elements(p08, "a")
href <- html_attr(a08[html_text2(a08) == "Statement"], "href")   # the 11 Statement links of 2008
unique(dirname(href))        # the folder part of the address: an older form
basename(href)               # the file part: two end in b
```

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

- The 2006 to 2010 pages link every statement in an older address form,
  `/newsevents/press/monetary/20060131a.htm`: 46 of the 129 Statement
  links. The server redirects each one to the current form,
  `/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20060131a.htm`. Lists built from
  different pages match only on the final address: save it.
- Three statement addresses end in `b` and the rest in `a`: 17 August
  2007, 22 January 2008, 16 December 2008. A rule that keeps only
  addresses ending in `a.htm`, which worked on the calendar, drops these
  three.

:::

- The brief to a coding agent

## The brief to the coding agent {#brief .smaller}

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

**Coding agent**: an AI tool that writes and runs code on your computer
from written instructions. Before class, one was run on the brief below,
in an empty folder. Permission to read, write and run files was given
before it started, so it never stopped to ask.

:::

```{.default filename="Terminal, in an empty folder holding brief.txt"}
$ ls
brief.txt
$ cat brief.txt
Collect every FOMC policy statement (the Federal Open Market Committee's statement on its
policy decision, issued after a scheduled meeting or an unscheduled call) from January 2006
to the latest one, from the Federal Reserve's website.

Start from the meeting calendar at https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomccalendars.htm
(2021 onward) and the one page per year at
https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomchistoricalYYYY.htm for 2006 to 2020.

Rules: send a user agent that identifies the request as "AEM 6850 class demo; <address>";
at most one request per second; save every page you fetch in cache/ and never fetch the same
page twice; if the server answers 429, wait and retry.

Write fomc_statements.csv with one row per statement and the columns date (YYYY-MM-DD), url
(the address after redirects), words, text (the statement's paragraphs only), scheduled
(TRUE after a scheduled meeting, FALSE after an unscheduled call). Use R. Print the number
of statements per year when you are done.
```

::: {style="font-size:0.7em"}

A brief names the unit and how to tell it apart, where to start, the
rules (user agent, pace, cache, retries), the output columns and the
numbers to print. This one never says which releases do not count; Part 5
shows what that cost.

:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
The pitfalls the brief leaves out: implementation notes, longer-run-goals
statements, the notation vote, the three b addresses, the liquidity and
swap-line releases.
:::

:::

## The demonstration: do marathon runners finish just under round times? {#demo-question .smaller}

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.8em"}

- **The question.** [Allen, Dechow, Pope & Wu (Management Science, 2017)](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2015.2417)
  found more finishers just under 3:00, 3:30 and 4:00 than just over, in
  9,789,093 marathon finish times. Runners treat round times as goals.
- **The pages.** The Wineglass Marathon in Corning, New York, an hour from
  Ithaca. Its timing company posts each year's results as one plain page:
  one line per finisher, with the **net time** (start line to finish line).
- **Allowed.** The site has no robots.txt (404) and no terms of use. The
  lines carry names, ages and towns: keep place, sex, age group and time.

:::

```{.default filename="leonetiming.com/2023/Roads/Wineglass/WGMarathonNet.htm, the column headings and one line; name, age and town masked here"}
                                       PLACES IN               NET    NET
PLACE NAME                    AGE  SEX  &      AGEGROUP        TIME   PACE  CITY ...
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  665 ··························   F# 264   41/129  F30-34   3:59:00  9:08  ······
```

::: {style="font-size:0.72em"}

The page is fixed-width text inside one `<pre>` element: a selector finds
the block, and each line is cut by position or by a pattern.

:::

## The brief the two agents get {#demo-brief .smaller}

```{.default filename="brief.txt, alone in an empty folder; one folder's copy ends 'Use R.', the other's 'Use Python.'"}
Collect the finish times of every finisher of the Wineglass Marathon (Corning, New York) for
each year whose results Leone Timing posts as a web page. Start from the year's page at
https://www.leonetiming.com/YEAR/Roads/Wineglass/ for YEAR from 2018 to 2025; some years have
no page (there was no race in 2020). On each year's page, follow the link to the marathon
results by net time (not the half marathon, not the relay).

Rules: send a user agent that identifies the request as "AEM 6850 class demo; <address>"; at
most one request per second; save every page you fetch in cache/ and never fetch the same page
twice; if the server answers 429, wait and retry. The pages list runners' names, ages and
towns: keep only place, sex, age group and net time, and never print or save names, even
while you study a page's layout.

Write wineglass.csv with one row per finisher and the columns year, place, sex, age_group,
net_time (h:mm:ss) and net_minutes. Draw wineglass.png: the number of finishers in each
one-minute bin of net time from 2:30 to 6:30, all years together, with vertical lines at 3:00,
3:30, 4:00 and 4:30. Draw wineglass_years.png: the number of finishers and the median net
time, by year.

When you are done, print: for each year, the number of rows you kept and the last place
number on that year's page; the number of finishers at 3:57, 3:58, 3:59, 4:00, 4:01 and 4:02
(minutes, all years); and the median net time by year.

Use R.
```

::: {style="font-size:0.72em"}

Both agents start now, side by side, with permission to read, write and
run files given up front. Part 6 reads what they produce. In prep each
took between 2 and 3 minutes.

:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
Run sheet. Before class: two terminal windows, side by side, in two empty
folders, wineglass-r and wineglass-py, each holding only its brief.txt
(your address in place of `<address>`; the Python copy ends "Use Python,
with the Python at ~/demo-py/bin/python"). In each window type, at this
slide:

claude --allowedTools "Bash,Read,Write,Edit,Glob,Grep" "$(cat brief.txt)"

Then go on with Part 4; glance back at the windows on the next slide.
Prep runs (19 October 2026, both started together): R 2 min 49 s and
2 min 22 s; Python 2 min 11 s and 2 min 15 s; 15 requests each; the two
files identical row for row, 11,466 finishers. If the site is down: copy
the saved pages (aem6850-agent-runs/final-r/cache) into each folder's
cache/ and the agents read them; the slides in Part 6 carry the prep run.
:::

:::

## R or Python for a scrape {#r-or-python .smaller}

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

| Step | R | Python |
|:------------------------|:------------------|:------------------|
| Send a request with a user agent, a pause and retries | `httr2` | `requests` |
| Pick elements out of HTML with CSS selectors | `rvest` | `BeautifulSoup`, `lxml` |
| Read a page whose scripts must run first | `read_html_live()` (with `chromote`) | `playwright`, `selenium` |
| Crawl many thousands of pages, pausing and resuming | a loop over a cached fetch | `scrapy` |

- Both send the same requests and read the same HTML. For tens or
  hundreds of pages, scrape in the language you analyse in.
- Python has more ready-made tools for very large crawls and for driving
  a browser.
- A coding agent writes either. The brief, the saved pages and the
  comparisons decide whether the file is right; Part 6 compares the two
  agents' files.

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

`read_html_live()` is marked experimental in rvest and needs the chromote
package and Chrome on the computer. Scrapy's `JOBDIR` setting lets a crawl
stop and resume, and its AutoThrottle extension adjusts the pause to the
server's replies. Python's standard library reads robots.txt
(`urllib.robotparser`); in R, the robotstxt package does.

:::

**AI browser agent**: a program that opens pages in your own browser and
reads them for an assistant.

- **Use it for**
  - a page you have never seen, to find which element holds the date
  - a handful of pages
  - pages behind your own login, where the terms allow
- **Why a loop collects every statement instead**
  - the agent takes seconds to a minute per page; the loop takes about a
    second
  - the agent keeps no copy of the page, so there is nothing to cite or
    re-run
  - the site's terms apply to it as to any program

## The agent's file compared with the statements file {#agent-vs-site .smaller}

::: {style="font-size:0.78em"}

Did the agent get the same statements as the statements file?
**The statements file** (`ours` in the code): `fomc_statements.csv`, 171
rows, built from the pages in `cache/` by the rule in `SOURCE.txt`.

:::

```{r}
#| label: agent-vs-site
#| filename: "R Console, in the 15-scraping folder; reads agent_run/fomc_statements.csv (the agent's run 1) and fomc_statements.csv (ours)"
agent <- read.csv("agent_run/fomc_statements.csv")
ours  <- read.csv("fomc_statements.csv")
c(agent = nrow(agent), ours = nrow(ours))
yr <- data.frame(year = 2006:2026)
yr$agent <- as.vector(table(substr(agent$date, 1, 4)))   # rows per year; substr(): characters 1 to 4
yr$ours  <- as.vector(table(substr(ours$date,  1, 4)))
print(yr[yr$agent != yr$ours, ], row.names = FALSE)      # the years that differ
```

::: {style="font-size:0.78em"}

- The four extra rows are the four dates the table flags: 10 August 2007,
  11 March 2008, 9 May 2010, 11 October 2019.
- Each is a press release the site links as a Statement. It announces a
  lending programme or the mechanics of a decision, not the committee's
  decision on the policy rate.

:::

## Three lists of one site disagree on what a statement is {#three-lists .smaller}

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.85em"}

- **The site's links** (the agent's rule): 175.
  - 129 links named Statement on the year pages, 46 named HTML on the
    calendar.
- **The press-release feed**: 179 titles contain "FOMC statement".
  - Five of them are in neither file.
- **The statements file's rule**, written in `SOURCE.txt`: 171.
  - A page counts when its title says "FOMC statement" and it announces
    the decision on the policy rate.

Write the rule down before you scrape, and reconcile every difference by
hand.

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

The five feed titles in neither file: the dollar swap lines (two
releases), the statement of longer-run goals and policy strategy, a
change of release times, and the policy normalization principles and
plans. The feed comparison in code:

```{r}
#| label: agent-vs-feed
#| purl: false
feed_url <- paste0("https://www.federalreserve.gov", fs$l)
substr(fs$t[!(feed_url %in% agent$url)], 1, 75)      # in the feed, not in the agent's file
agent$date[!(agent$url %in% feed_url)]               # in the agent's file, not in the feed's set
```

:::

## Three statements drawn with a seed {#seeded-draw .smaller}

::: {style="font-size:0.78em"}

The counts match on most years; does the text match? **Seed**: a starting
number that makes a random draw repeat on every computer, so the room
draws the same three rows and reads them against the statements file.

::::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="40%"}

![](figures/15-scraping/S06-statement-20081029.png){fig-align="center" fig-alt="The statement page of 29 October 2008: the date, the title FOMC statement, For immediate release, four paragraphs of text, the voting paragraph and the Board's related discount-rate action."}

::: {.column width="60%"}

```{r}
#| label: seeded-draw
#| filename: "R Console; needs agent and ours, read on the counts slide"
set.seed(6850)
pick <- sample(nrow(agent), 3)
agent[pick, c("date", "words", "scheduled")]
# match(): the row of ours with the same date
agent$text[pick] == ours$text[match(agent$date[pick], ours$date)]
# the last row, so the scrape ran to the end
agent[nrow(agent), c("date", "words")]
```

::: {style="font-size:0.72em"}

The screenshot is the 29 October 2008 page, the third row drawn. In both
files its text starts at the first paragraph; the page header and the
link to the implementation note are left out. The three TRUEs say the
agent's text and the statements file's text are identical on those three
dates.

:::::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
The latest statement opens with its vote ("approved the following
statement for release by a 12 – 0 vote"); older ones end with a voting
paragraph. Both files date the June 2007 statement 28 June from the
page's own date line, where the address says 0618: the address carries a
typo. The January 2012 row is the policy statement (20120125a), not the

## The agent's 429 count, read from its own log {#agent-log .smaller}

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

The agent said four 429 replies came. The log it wrote records every
request. **The claim**, from its closing message: "The server returned
429 four times, and each request was retried and then succeeded."

:::

```{r}
#| label: agent-log
#| filename: "R Console, in the 15-scraping folder; reads agent_run/fetch_log.txt"
fetch_log <- readLines("agent_run/fetch_log.txt")
c(lines = length(fetch_log), fetched = sum(startsWith(fetch_log, "fetched")))
sub("fetched https://www.federalreserve.gov", "", grep("429", fetch_log, value = TRUE))   # the lines that contain 429
```

::: {style="font-size:0.78em"}

The agent counted the lines that contain 429 with the shell command
`grep -c 429 fetch_log.txt` and got 4. Those four lines are fetches of
statements dated 29 April: each address holds `0429`. Every line in the
log is a successful fetch. No 429 reply came.

**Takeaway:** a number in an agent's summary is a claim about its files.
Read the files before you repeat it.

:::

[The log holds 172 of the 191 fetches. The agent fetched the 16 list
pages and three statements before it started the log; all 191 pages are
in its cache/.]{.source}

```{r}
#| label: demo-compare
```
